messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 77
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Firefighter
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 40

He is seventy-seven now, a retired firefighter who still wakes before dawn as if the station alarm might sound. He lives with his wife in a small, tidy house, and when he talks about his life he does so carefully, as if opening drawers that have been shut for many years. He came to the United States from Southeast Asia decades ago, but when he begins at the beginning, he is again a young man in a civilian neighborhood turned into a war zone, not a soldier, just a son and brother trying to keep his family alive.

He remembers the war first through sound. Before he speaks of blood or bodies, he speaks of the whistle overhead, the split second of silence, then the blast that seemed to lift the ground. He is a teenager then, carrying water and rice, learning to tell from far away whether gunfire is moving closer or farther from home. He says everyone around him learned to live inside constant readiness. Meals were interrupted, sleep was shallow, and every ordinary task came with calculation: where to run, who to grab, what could be left behind. One afternoon an explosion hits near the street where he and his family are sheltering. He does not tell the story dramatically. He says he remembers dust so thick he cannot see his own hands, remembers his mother screaming for one of his siblings, remembers stepping over someone on the ground and refusing to look down because if he looked, he might stop moving. In the days after, there are bodies in places where children used to play. The smell of smoke and burned metal gets into clothing, food, hair, skin.

What stays with him most is not one single incident but the way fear becomes the structure of daily life. He learns to scan rooftops, listen for engines, count exits in every room. At night he lies awake waiting for the next impact. If he does sleep, he wakes confused and already running inside himself. He sees neighbors disappear, hears rumors of arrests and killings, and lives with the steady knowledge that civilians can die at any moment for no reason they control. Even after he and his family eventually escape, his body does not understand that escape means safety.

In America, he works hard, learns the language he can, and chooses a job that makes sense to him in a way he cannot fully explain at first. He becomes a firefighter. People tell him he is calm in emergencies. He is proud of that. Inside danger, he knows exactly what to do: check the exits, read the smoke, move toward the trapped person, keep his voice steady. The structure suits him, and so does the brotherhood. Yet the work also keeps him close to the same sounds and smells that have followed him from the war. The backfire of an engine, the sudden crack of something bursting in a fire, the heat against his face, the smell of burning insulation—these can pull him abruptly into another time. He never panics outwardly. Instead, he goes rigid, jaw clenched, breathing through his nose until the moment passes. After difficult calls, younger men go for coffee and joke to shake it off; he goes home quiet and sits alone in the garage before entering the house.

His wife has known for years that sleep is difficult for him. He kicks in his sleep, sometimes shouts in a language he speaks less and less during the day. There are nights he wakes soaked in sweat, heart pounding, sure for a few seconds that the house is under attack. He checks the windows and doors, sometimes more than once, though he knows the neighborhood is safe. Fireworks are worst. On holidays he keeps the television louder than necessary to cover the popping outside, but still his shoulders tense and his eyes narrow, tracking each burst. His grandchildren once laughed when he ducked at a sudden bang in the driveway, and he laughed too, embarrassed, though later he stayed inside the rest of the evening.

He does not like crowds because he needs to know where every exit is, and he prefers restaurants where he can sit facing the door. He says this as if it is merely habit, but if his wife suggests switching seats, he becomes uneasy and distracted for the rest of the meal. He avoids news footage of bombings and avoids talking in detail about the war with his children, who know only fragments. For many years he told himself that surviving meant not looking back. Still, memories arrive uninvited: the dust cloud, his mother’s voice, the feeling of stepping over a body and continuing to run.

Now, in older age and retirement, there are fewer distractions. Without the rhythm of shifts and alarms, the past has more room to speak. He finds himself sitting in the early morning stillness, listening for sounds that are not there. He is grateful for his life, for his marriage, for the family he helped build, but he says some part of him never left that street. Even now, in a quiet house in peacetime, his body waits for impact.
